draft.title: Urban renewal and gentrification
card: the redevelopment of an older, run-down urban area. It can mean new housing, upgraded public spaces and the reuse of old factories or warehouses.
a change in who lives in an area, as wealthier residents move into a lower-income area. It often follows renewal, but the two are not the same thing.
As demand from wealthier people grows, rents and house prices tend to rise. Shops and cafés change to suit the new residents.

Long-term residents on lower incomes may be pushed out when they can no longer afford the rent or the rates. Some benefit instead, for example from better services or a rise in the value of a home they own.
draft.remember: Renewal rebuilds an area. Gentrification changes who lives there, and rising costs can push some people out.

opts: Wealthier residents moving into a lower-income area
Old buildings in a city area being demolished
A city spreading outwards onto farmland
People moving from rural areas to a city
a.why: Gentrification is about a change in who lives in an area, as wealthier people move in. Demolishing old buildings is part of renewal, which is tempting but is about the buildings, not the residents.
a.clue: Focus on who lives in the area, not the buildings.

b.q: An old dockside area in a coastal city is renewed with new apartments and a park. Rents double over five years. Which outcome is most likely for a low-income renter there?
opts: They may be unable to afford the higher rent and move out
They will be forced to leave by the government
They will see their rent fall as services improve
They will gain, because renewal lifts all incomes
b.why: When wealthier residents arrive, demand and rents rise, so a low-income renter may no longer afford to stay. Renewal does not always lift incomes, and the card says people may be pushed out by costs, not that anyone is forced by the government.
b.clue: Think about what rising rents do to people on lower incomes.

a.best: Wealthier residents moving into a lower-income area

b.best: They may be unable to afford the higher rent and move out

problems.detail: The right option is the longest and the only one hedged with 'may'. The three distractors all say 'will'. A student could pick it from its form alone, without knowing the idea.

b.q: An old dockside area in a coastal city is renewed with new apartments and a park. Rents double over five years. Which outcome is most likely for a low-income renter there?
opts: Struggling to pay the rent and moving out of the area
Gaining from a rise in the value of their home
Paying lower rent as new apartments add supply
Finding local shops change to suit low-income people
b.why: As wealthier people move in, demand pushes rents up, so a low-income renter may no longer afford to stay. A rise in home values helps people who own their home, but a renter does not own one, so that gain does not reach them.
b.clue: Does a renter own the home they live in?
